options.D: Determining the financial cost of radiation therapy equipment for the hospital

explanation: Nurses spend the most time with patients, giving them unique insights into daily symptoms, goals, and fears that shape the care plan. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h7)

question: During which specific phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur?

options.A: G2 phase
options.B: G1 phase
options.C: S phase
options.D: M phase

explanation: The synthesis or S phase is dedicated entirely to replicating the cell's genetic material prior to division. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the primary function of cell cycle checkpoints?

options.A: To accelerate the production of metabolic energy
options.B: To halt division and allow for DNA damage repair
options.C: To permanently lock the cell in the mitotic phase
options.D: To stimulate rapid and unregulated tissue growth

explanation: Checkpoints serve as surveillance mechanisms that pause the cycle to detect and correct errors before replication proceeds. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which cellular adaptation describes the reversible replacement of one adult cell type by another?

options.A: Anaplasia
options.B: Metaplasia
options.C: Dysplasia
options.D: Hyperplasia

explanation: Metaplasia occurs when chronic stress prompts tissue to substitute a hardier cell type for a more vulnerable one. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: A patient's biopsy report indicates disordered cellular growth with significant variation in nuclear size and shape, categorized as a pre-malignant lesion. Which term best fits this description?

options.A: Hyperplasia
options.B: Dysplasia
options.C: Metaplasia
options.D: Apoptosis

explanation: Dysplasia denotes disordered growth and loss of uniformity, representing an intermediate step toward malignancy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the primary characteristic that distinguishes a malignant tumor from a benign tumor?

options.A: Having a well-defined fibrous capsule
options.B: Cells that closely resemble the tissue of origin
options.C: The ability to metastasize to distant sites
options.D: A very slow and predictable growth rate

explanation: Metastasis is the hallmark of malignancy, allowing cancer cells to invade blood vessels and establish secondary colonies elsewhere in the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: A histopathology report describes a tumor as having poorly differentiated cells with irregular borders and deep infiltration into adjacent muscular layers. How should this neoplasm be classified?

options.A: Benign
options.B: Malignant
options.C: Hyperplastic
options.D: Metaplastic

explanation: Poor differentiation and local tissue invasion are definitive indicators of a malignant neoplasm. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: What defines the unique capability of stem cells known as self-renewal?

options.A: The rapid conversion of mature somatic cells into fully functional neurons
options.B: The ability to undergo numerous divisions while maintaining an unspecialized state
options.C: The transformation of malignant tissues into benign structural counterparts
options.D: The spontaneous induction of programmed cell death when DNA is damaged

explanation: Self-renewal ensures that the stem cell pool remains replenished throughout the life of the organism while continuously supplying differentiated progeny. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why do cancer stem cells pose a significant challenge in oncology treatment?

options.A: They lose all capacity for cell division once primary treatment begins
options.B: They frequently survive conventional therapies and drive tumor recurrence
options.C: They secrete chemical signals that convert malignant cells into benign ones
options.D: They undergo rapid apoptosis upon exposure to pharmaceutical agents

explanation: Cancer stem cells often exhibit high resistance to chemotherapy and radiation, allowing them to regenerate the tumor even after apparent clinical remission. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary underlying cause of genetic alterations in cancer cells?

options.A: Excessive production of normal structural proteins by ribosomes
options.B: Inactivation of all metabolic pathways within mitochondria
options.C: Permanent cessation of the cell cycle during the G1 phase
options.D: Accumulation of DNA mutations in somatic cells over time

explanation: Cancer arises from sequential genetic mutations that disrupt normal cell cycle controls and DNA repair mechanisms. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: What clinical implication arises from tumor heterogeneity during chemotherapy?

options.A: All cancer cells within the tumor mass respond identically to the medication
options.B: Certain sub-populations of cancer cells may be resistant to the drug and survive
options.C: Metastasis becomes completely impossible due to genetic stabilization
options.D: The tumor will spontaneously convert into a benign, self-limiting growth

explanation: Because different cells within the same tumor have distinct mutations, targeted therapies may kill some cells while drug-resistant variants survive and proliferate. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the normal physiological role of proto-oncogenes in healthy tissue?

options.A: To induce immediate programmed cell death upon detecting DNA errors
options.B: To halt the cell cycle when chromosomal damage is irreparable
options.C: To replace damaged epithelial cells with fibrous connective tissue
options.D: To encode proteins that stimulate normal cell growth and division

explanation: Proto-oncogenes are essential normal genes that regulate positive growth signaling until mutations convert them into hyperactive oncogenes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: According to the two-hit hypothesis, why do most hereditary cancer syndromes require inactivation of both gene alleles?

options.A: A single functional copy of a tumor suppressor gene is often sufficient to maintain normal cell cycle control
options.B: Immune surveillance destroys cells that have only lost one copy of a regulatory gene
options.C: Both alleles must be amplified simultaneously to induce rapid cellular differentiation
options.D: Oncogenes require double mutations to prevent normal apoptotic pathways from engaging

explanation: Tumor suppressors are recessive at the cellular level, meaning both copies must be knocked out before their growth-restraining function is lost. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: Which key group of enzymes acts as the primary executioner cascade during apoptosis?

options.A: Histone deacetylases
options.B: Caspases
options.C: Proto-oncogenes
options.D: Cyclin-dependent kinases

explanation: Caspases are proteolytic enzymes that systematically break down cellular proteins during programmed cell death. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of apoptosis?

options.A: Systematic and energy-dependent dismantling of cellular proteins
options.B: Spillover of cellular contents causing local tissue inflammation
options.C: Controlled condensation of chromatin within the nucleus
options.D: Formation of membrane-bound apoptotic bodies for phagocytosis

explanation: Apoptosis is specifically designed to clear cells cleanly without spilling contents, which prevents the inflammation characteristic of accidental necrosis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why do traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy agents frequently cause side effects such as alopecia and mucositis?

options.A: They selectively stimulate apoptosis in benign connective tissue throughout the body
options.B: They convert malignant cells into metaplastic tissue within the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: They indiscriminately target rapidly dividing healthy cells in hair follicles and mucosal linings
options.D: They permanently deactivate all stem cell niches located within the bone marrow

explanation: Conventional chemotherapy affects any rapidly proliferating tissue, leading to common toxicities in hair, skin, and mucosal surfaces. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h8)

question: How do modern targeted cancer therapies differ fundamentally from traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy?

options.A: Targeted therapies eliminate cancer by inducing rapid, uncontrolled necrosis in all tissues
options.B: Targeted therapies exclusively use radiation beams focused on the primary tumor capsule
options.C: Targeted therapies aim at specific molecular abnormalities in cancer cells rather than all dividing cells
options.D: Targeted therapies rely entirely on preventing the expression of normal proto-oncogenes

explanation: Targeted drugs block specific proteins or genes involved in cancer growth, reducing collateral damage to normal, healthy tissues compared to broad cytotoxic drugs. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary biological driver behind the formation of a neoplasm?

options.A: Accelerated physiological tissue repair
options.B: Permanent cessation of the cell cycle
options.C: Genetic mutations disrupting cell division
options.D: Chronic bacterial infection of soft tissue

explanation: Neoplasms arise when mutations alter DNA, causing cells to proliferate uncontrollably without normal regulatory checks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do growing neoplastic tissues often outpace the metabolic health of surrounding normal structures?

options.A: They actively destroy vital nutrients before absorption
options.B: They physically block all oxygen transport pathways
options.C: They compete aggressively for local blood supply and nutrients
options.D: They secrete toxins that paralyze nearby healthy cells

explanation: Rapidly dividing cancer cells demand high amounts of energy and oxygen, redirecting resources away from adjacent healthy tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which structural feature typically separates a benign tumor from surrounding healthy tissue?

options.A: An influx of lymphocytes
options.B: A dense vascular network
options.C: A layer of necrotic cells
options.D: A fibrous capsule

explanation: Benign growths are usually surrounded by a distinct fibrous capsule that keeps them localized and distinct from adjacent tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: What makes a benign tumor clinically dangerous despite its non-cancerous nature?

options.A: It can compress vital organs due to its location
options.B: It rapidly mutates into an aggressive carcinoma
options.C: It releases systemic toxins into the bloodstream
options.D: It consistently destroys surrounding lymph nodes

explanation: Even without spreading, space-occupying benign growths can disrupt function by pressing against delicate structures like the brain or spinal cord. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: What term describes the lack of cellular differentiation and primitive appearance seen in malignant cells?

options.A: Metaplasia
options.B: Apoptosis
options.C: Anaplasia
options.D: Hypertrophy

explanation: Anaplasia refers to the regression of cells to a more immature, undifferentiated state, which is a hallmark of malignant tumors. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h3)

question: Which process enables malignant cells to establish secondary colonies in distant organs?

options.A: Hyperplasia
options.B: Metastasis
options.C: Encapsulation
options.D: Necrosis

explanation: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the primary site to distant parts of the body via blood vessels or lymphatics. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h3)

question: An osteosarcoma originates from which primary tissue type?

options.A: Epithelial lining of internal organs
options.B: Glandular secretory epithelium
options.C: Blood-forming bone marrow cells
options.D: Connective and supportive tissue

explanation: Sarcomas are malignant neoplasms that arise from mesenchymal tissues, which include bone, muscle, cartilage, and fat. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which category represents the most common type of malignant tumor found in adults?

options.A: Leukemias
options.B: Sarcomas
options.C: Carcinomas
options.D: Lymphomas

explanation: Carcinomas arise from epithelial cells, which line body surfaces and cavities, making them the most frequent type of adult cancer. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h4)

question: What does tumor grading primarily evaluate?

options.A: The extent of regional lymph node involvement
options.B: The microscopic appearance and differentiation of cells
options.C: The presence of metastasis in distant body organs
options.D: The physical size and location of the primary mass

explanation: Grading is a pathological assessment focused on cellular characteristics and how closely they resemble normal tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h5)

question: In the TNM staging system, what does the letter 'N' stand for?

options.A: Nuclear atypia score
options.B: Necrosis of the core tissue
options.C: Regional lymph node involvement
options.D: Number of mitotic figures

explanation: In cancer staging, the 'N' category measures whether and how extensively the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary clinical consequence of myelosuppression induced by chemotherapy?

options.A: Enlargement of peripheral lymph nodes
options.B: Rapid regeneration of liver tissue
options.C: Depression of bone marrow activity
options.D: Hyperactivity of the endocrine system

explanation: Myelosuppression refers to the suppression of blood cell production in the bone marrow, leading to low counts of red cells, white cells, and platelets. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h6)

question: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops severe thrombocytopenia. Which nursing intervention is most critical for this patient?

options.A: Monitoring closely for signs of abnormal bleeding
options.B: Encouraging vigorous physical exercise to boost energy
options.C: Administering large doses of oral iron supplements
options.D: Implementing strict neutropenic isolation precautions

explanation: Thrombocytopenia means a low platelet count, which impairs blood clotting and places the patient at high risk for hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is the primary characteristic of neoplastic cellular proliferation?

options.A: Temporary hyperplasia resolving after injury
options.B: Autonomous and uncoordinated growth
options.C: Synchronized division with surrounding tissue
options.D: Reversible expansion driven by hormones

explanation: Neoplasms grow independently of normal physiological regulatory stimuli, distinguishing them from adaptive cellular changes like hypertrophy or hyperplasia. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which cellular checkpoint failure directly contributes to the accumulation of mutations in cancer cells?

options.A: Bypassing the G1/S cell cycle arrest
options.B: Enhanced ribosomal RNA transcription rates
options.C: Excessive activation of intercellular gap junctions
options.D: Premature shedding of the nuclear membrane

explanation: Failing to arrest at the G1/S transition allows cells with damaged DNA to replicate their genetic material instead of undergoing repair or apoptosis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which structural feature is most commonly associated with benign neoplasms?

options.A: Widespread metastasis
options.B: Microvascular invasion
options.C: Anaplastic borders
options.D: A fibrous capsule

explanation: Benign tumors typically develop a surrounding fibrous capsule that limits their expansion and prevents local tissue invasion. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h2)

question: A biopsy report describes a tumor as well-differentiated with no evidence of capsule invasion. How should the nurse interpret this finding?

options.A: The lesion shares many microscopic features with parent tissue and behaves non-invasively.
options.B: The patient requires immediate emergency radiation therapy for metastasis.
options.C: The cells have completely lost their original tissue identity and spread rapidly.
options.D: The mass has activated neoangiogenesis to recruit distant blood supplies.

explanation: Well-differentiated cells closely resemble the normal mature tissue of origin, which strongly points toward a benign classification. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is the normal physiological function of proto-oncogenes in healthy tissue?

options.A: Promoting normal cellular growth and division
options.B: Synthesizing fibrous stroma around blood vessels
options.C: Encapsulating local tissue to prevent expansion
options.D: Inducing prompt apoptosis upon minor DNA stress

explanation: Proto-oncogenes regulate normal growth pathways; they only drive cancer when mutated into hyperactive oncogenes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h3)

question: What happens when both alleles of a critical tumor suppressor gene suffer inactivating mutations?

options.A: Cell cycle progression is permanently arrested in G0.
options.B: The cell immediately undergoes spontaneous necrosis.
options.C: Cellular replication loses a vital regulatory brake.
options.D: Intracellular repair mechanisms become hyperactive.

explanation: Tumor suppressor genes act as brakes on division; losing both alleles removes these controls, allowing uncontrolled proliferation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h3)

question: Which phase of carcinogenesis involves a permanent, irreversible alteration of cellular DNA?

options.A: Initiation
options.B: Regression
options.C: Angiogenesis
options.D: Promotion

explanation: Initiation is the first irreversible step where a mutagenic agent damages the cellular DNA structure. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h4)

question: A patient with a history of tobacco use is advised that continued exposure to certain chemical irritants accelerates tumor development even without causing direct DNA mutations. Which stage of carcinogenesis does this describe?

options.A: Promotion
options.B: Initiation
options.C: Apoptosis
options.D: Metastasis

explanation: Promotion involves agents that stimulate cell division and expand the population of previously initiated cells without directly mutating DNA. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h4)

question: Which specific factor is primarily responsible for stimulating new blood vessel growth in growing tumors?

options.A: Transforming growth factor beta
options.B: Platelet-derived structural protein
options.C: Vascular endothelial growth factor
options.D: Epithelial basement membrane kinase

explanation: Tumor cells secrete vascular endothelial growth factor to signal surrounding endothelial cells to build new capillary networks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why must a malignant neoplasm stimulate neoangiogenesis once it reaches a certain size?

options.A: The lymphatic system physically blocks further horizontal expansion.
options.B: Host immune cells require direct vascular access to enter the core.
options.C: Passive diffusion can no longer supply nutrients and oxygen to deep cells.
options.D: Normal capillaries actively secrete suppressive matrix proteins.

explanation: Diffusion is limited to short distances, forcing tumors to build dedicated blood vessels to avoid central hypoxia and necrosis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which enzyme group is utilized by cancer cells to degrade the extracellular matrix during local invasion?

options.A: Cyclin-dependent transferases
options.B: Intracellular caspases
options.C: Matrix metalloproteinases
options.D: Vascular endothelial kinases

explanation: Matrix metalloproteinases break down collagen and structural barriers, allowing malignant cells to breach tissue planes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h6)

question: What happens when epithelial cancer cells lose the expression of cell adhesion molecules such as E-cadherin?

options.A: They separate easily from neighboring cells and gain mobility.
options.B: They form tight fibrous capsules to restrict local expansion.
options.C: They revert to a benign, well-differentiated phenotype.
options.D: They immediately undergo programmed apoptosis due to stress.

explanation: E-cadherin keeps epithelial cells tightly bound; losing it reduces cell-to-cell adhesion, facilitating detachment and migration. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h6)

question: What term describes the systemic wasting syndrome characterized by profound muscle loss and weakness in advanced cancer?

options.A: Metaplasia
options.B: Cachexia
options.C: Anaplasia
options.D: Cacheting

explanation: Cancer cachexia involves severe muscle and fat depletion driven by tumor-induced metabolic changes and systemic inflammation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h7)

question: Which of the following describes a paraneoplastic syndrome?

options.A: Acute bone marrow failure caused by direct pharmacological toxicity from chemotherapy
options.B: Direct physical compression of a peripheral nerve by an enlarging fibrous capsule
options.C: The localized necrosis occurring at the center of an unvascularized tumor core
options.D: Systemic symptoms triggered by tumor hormone secretions rather than direct mass effect

explanation: Paraneoplastic syndromes arise when tumors produce ectopic hormones or peptides that disrupt normal host physiology at distant sites. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary objective of control therapy in oncology?

options.A: Achieve complete eradication of malignant cells
options.B: Provide total symptom relief without extending life
options.C: Halt disease progression and manage tumor burden
options.D: Prevent the initial genetic mutation of cells

explanation: Control therapy focuses on keeping the cancer from spreading further and reducing the tumor size when a complete cure is not possible. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h1)

question: A patient with widespread, incurable metastasis is admitted for pain control and comfort measures. Which treatment goal is guiding this care plan?

options.A: Adjuvant
options.B: Preventive
options.C: Palliative
options.D: Curative

explanation: Palliative care prioritizes comfort and quality of life when the disease can no longer be cured or controlled. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h1)

question: The primary purpose of a diagnostic surgical biopsy in oncology is to...

options.A: Completely eradicate the primary tumor site
options.B: Obtain tissue samples for histological confirmation
options.C: Remove organs at high genetic risk of malignancy
options.D: Relieve acute obstruction and severe hemorrhage

explanation: Diagnostic surgery directly samples tumor tissue so pathologists can confirm the exact cell type and cancer stage. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h2)

question: Why would a surgeon perform a debulking procedure for a patient with an advanced, incurable tumor?

options.A: To relieve pressure on surrounding vital structures and reduce pain
options.B: To completely cure the patient by removing all microscopic traces
options.C: To stimulate the patient's immune system to attack remaining cells
options.D: To prevent the original tumor cells from mutating into a new cancer

explanation: Debulking is a palliative measure that lessens the physical burden of a large tumor mass to improve the patient's comfort. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary mechanism by which radiation therapy destroys cancer cells?

options.A: Stimulating the patient's white blood cells
options.B: Altering the systemic pH of the body
options.C: Damaging cellular DNA to cause cell death
options.D: Blocking the blood supply to the tumor bed

explanation: Ionizing radiation directly breaks down the genetic material within cells, halting their ability to divide and survive. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h3)

question: Which instruction is essential for a nurse to provide to a patient receiving external beam radiation to the neck?

options.A: Apply a tight synthetic bandage to protect the skin from sunlight
options.B: Scrub the skin markings vigorously with an antiseptic sponge daily
options.C: Use heating pads frequently on the neck to relieve muscle stiffness
options.D: Avoid applying commercial lotions or perfumes to the marked treatment area

explanation: Substances like lotions can react with radiation or trap heat on the skin, worsening burns; skin markings must also be preserved and never scrubbed off. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the primary risk associated with the extravasation of a vesicant chemotherapy agent?

options.A: Severe local tissue necrosis and sloughing
options.B: Rapid elevation of systemic blood pressure
options.C: Immediate systemic allergic anaphylaxis
options.D: Permanent damage to the cardiac muscle

explanation: Vesicants are blistering agents that cause severe, destructive damage to subcutaneous tissues if they leak outside the vein. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h4)

question: A patient receiving outpatient chemotherapy calls the clinic reporting a temperature of 38.5°C. What is the most appropriate initial nursing instruction?

options.A: Drink plenty of cold fluids and recheck the temperature in six hours
options.B: Apply a cold compress to the forehead to bring the fever down safely
options.C: Report immediately to the emergency facility for a full sepsis workup
options.D: Take an extra dose of prescribed oral vitamins and rest at home

explanation: Fever in a neutropenic patient is an oncological emergency indicating potential sepsis, requiring immediate medical evaluation and broad-spectrum antibiotics. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h4)

question: How do targeted therapies differ fundamentally from traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy?

options.A: They focus on specific molecular pathways unique to cancer cells
options.B: They exclusively target normal rapidly dividing mucosal cells
options.C: They only work when administered directly into the spinal column
options.D: They completely eliminate the need for any supportive nursing care

explanation: Targeted agents are designed to interfere with specific molecules needed for tumor growth, rather than targeting all dividing cells indiscriminately. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the underlying cause of immune-related adverse events during immunotherapy?

options.A: Bacterial contamination of the intravenous medication bag
options.B: Enhanced immune activity attacking normal healthy organs
options.C: Direct toxic destruction of bone marrow stem cells
options.D: Severe allergic hypersensitivity to synthetic preservatives

explanation: By taking the brakes off the immune system, immunotherapy can prompt T-cells to attack healthy host tissues, causing inflammatory side effects. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which electrolyte imbalances are classic hallmarks of tumor lysis syndrome?

options.A: Hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia
options.B: Hypokalemia and hypocalcemia
options.C: Hyponatremia and hypermagnesemia
options.D: Hypophosphatemia and hypernatremia

explanation: The massive lysis of cancer cells releases large amounts of intracellular potassium and phosphate directly into the circulation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h6)

question: A patient with lung cancer develops facial swelling, engorged neck veins, and shortness of breath. Which oncological emergency is most likely occurring?

options.A: Tumor lysis syndrome
options.B: Hypercalcemic crisis
options.C: Spinal cord compression
options.D: Superior vena cava syndrome

explanation: Obstruction or compression of the superior vena cava impairs venous return from the upper body, producing characteristic facial and neck edema. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of the World Health Organization analgesic ladder in cancer care?

options.A: To calculate the exact chemotherapy dose required for tumor regression
options.B: To guide a systematic, step-wise approach to pain management
options.C: To determine the safe timeline for radiation therapy fractionation
options.D: To measure the functional status and mobility of palliative patients

explanation: The WHO ladder helps clinicians select appropriate pain medications based on pain severity, escalating from non-opioids to strong opioids as needed. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why is it important to administer antiemetic medications proactively before a patient receives moderately emetogenic chemotherapy?

options.A: It prevents the direct physical rupture of gastrointestinal blood vessels
options.B: Proactive dosing eliminates the risk of developing total bone marrow failure
options.C: Antiemetics lose all chemical stability if taken after vomiting begins
options.D: It is significantly easier to prevent nausea than to stop it once it has started

explanation: Preventative antiemetic therapy blocks neurotransmitter pathways before they are triggered by chemotherapy agents, offering far superior control. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h7)

question: At what point in the disease trajectory should palliative care ideally be introduced for a patient with cancer?

options.A: Strictly when the patient is discharged home without nursing support
options.B: Only after all curative chemotherapy options have completely failed
options.C: Exclusively during the final twenty-four hours of active dying
options.D: Alongside disease-directed treatment early in the course of illness

explanation: Modern guidelines recommend integrating palliative care early to manage symptoms and distress concurrently with active cancer treatments. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h8)

question: Which nursing action best demonstrates effective psychosocial support for a newly diagnosed oncology patient?

options.A: Assuring the family that the patient will definitely be cured with modern therapy
options.B: Focusing exclusively on physical vital signs to prevent emotional overwhelm
options.C: Directing the patient to avoid discussing emotional worries to maintain optimism
options.D: Providing a safe space for the patient and family to express fears and ask questions

explanation: Open communication and validating emotional distress are core components of compassionate, holistic psychosocial nursing care. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary objective of systemic medical interventions in cancer care?

options.A: To permanently replace damaged bone marrow cells with donor tissue
options.B: To reach and destroy circulating malignant cells and micrometastases
options.C: To provide immediate mechanical decompression of compressed nerves
options.D: To physically remove localized solid tumors from healthy organs

explanation: Systemic treatments travel through the bloodstream to target cancer cells wherever they have spread in the body, unlike localized interventions such as surgery. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why do many oncology patients in resource-constrained settings frequently require systemic medical therapies as their initial treatment?

options.A: Systemic medications are consistently more affordable than localized surgical procedures
options.B: Pathology laboratories lack the capacity to identify specific histological tumor types
options.C: Surgical oncologists are entirely unavailable outside of metropolitan teaching hospitals
options.D: They present predominantly with advanced-stage disease requiring widespread systemic control

explanation: Delayed presentation often results in widespread metastasis, making systemic agents necessary to address disease beyond the reach of local surgery. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why do cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs cause damage to normal, healthy tissues in the body?

options.A: They cause direct thermal injury to blood vessels during intravenous infusion
options.B: They trigger an aggressive autoimmune response against healthy organs
options.C: They bind permanently to hemoglobin molecules and reduce tissue oxygenation
options.D: They specifically target any rapidly dividing cells regardless of malignancy

explanation: Cytotoxic agents cannot distinguish between rapidly dividing cancer cells and normal fast-growing cells like bone marrow and gut lining. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h2)

question: What is the primary reason for administering vesicant chemotherapy agents through a verified central venous catheter instead of a peripheral vein?

options.A: To completely eliminate the risk of systemic infection during prolonged treatment
options.B: To accelerate the renal excretion rate and minimize systemic drug accumulation
options.C: To prevent severe local tissue necrosis if the medication leaks into subcutaneous tissue
options.D: To allow the patient to self-administer maintenance doses at home without supervision

explanation: Vesicants cause blistering and deep tissue destruction; central lines ensure safer delivery into high-flow blood vessels where dilution is rapid. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h2)

question: How do targeted therapy drugs differ fundamentally from traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy?

options.A: They focus on specific molecular alterations and pathways driving tumor growth
options.B: They destroy all rapidly dividing cells indiscriminately throughout the body
options.C: They are administered only via continuous subcutaneous infusion pumps
options.D: They rely exclusively on stimulating the patient's T-lymphocytes

explanation: Targeted therapies zero in on specific proteins or genes unique to the cancer cells, sparing many normal tissues affected by standard chemotherapy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary mechanism of action for immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer treatment?

options.A: Binding directly to intracellular DNA to prevent double-strand replication during mitosis
options.B: Inhibiting hormone receptors on breast tissue to starve estrogen-dependent cancer cells
options.C: Blocking proteins that put the brakes on immune responses, allowing T-cells to attack tumors
options.D: Creating localized thermal coagulation necrosis within solid organ tumor masses

explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors remove inhibitory signals that tumors use to evade detection, re-engaging the patient's immune system to fight the malignancy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h3)

question: Which malignancies are most frequently treated using hormone therapy modalities?

options.A: Breast and prostate cancers
options.B: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
options.C: Glioblastoma multiforme
options.D: Squamous cell lung cancer

explanation: Breast and prostate cancers frequently rely on estrogen and androgen hormones respectively to drive their growth and proliferation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h4)

question: A patient undergoing long-term hormone therapy for prostate cancer reports progressive joint pain and decreased bone density. What physiological process explains this finding?

options.A: Rapid cellular division in osteoclasts causes excessive cartilage destruction
options.B: Direct monoclonal antibody binding triggers localized synovial inflammation
options.C: Cytotoxic bone marrow suppression leads to immediate trabecular bone necrosis
options.D: Androgen deprivation reduces bone mineral density and accelerates skeletal demineralization

explanation: Suppressing sex hormones alters bone remodeling balance, leading to long-term complications like osteopenia and osteoporosis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h4)

question: What is the fundamental mechanism by which radiation therapy destroys malignant tissues?

options.A: Blocking peripheral hormone receptor sites on the cell membrane
options.B: Stimulating the patient's T-cells to mount a cell-mediated immune response
options.C: Inducing systemic hepatic enzyme degradation of circulating nutrients
options.D: Damaging intracellular DNA to halt cell division and trigger apoptosis

explanation: Ionizing radiation creates free radicals that break chemical bonds in DNA, ultimately causing cell death or preventing replication. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h5)

question: Which instruction should be included in the skin care plan for a patient receiving external beam radiation therapy?

options.A: Apply heating pads to the irradiated skin area to relieve localized muscular stiffness
options.B: Avoid applying lotions, perfumes, or adhesive tape to the treatment markings and irradiated skin
options.C: Expose the treatment field to direct sunlight for short periods to promote healing
options.D: Scrub the treatment field vigorously daily with a coarse washcloth and medicated soap

explanation: Substances like lotions can trap heat or alter radiation dosage absorption, while adhesive tape can further damage fragile irradiated skin. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h5)

question: What hematological condition resulting from chemotherapy places a patient at the highest risk for life-threatening opportunistic infections?

options.A: Polycythemia
options.B: Erythrocytosis
options.C: Neutropenia
options.D: Thrombocytopenia

explanation: A severe drop in neutrophils reduces the body's primary defense against bacterial and fungal pathogens, requiring strict infection control. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h6)

question: A patient receiving neurotoxic chemotherapy reports progressive numbness and tingling in their fingers and toes. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Apply tight compression bandages to the distal extremities to stabilize nerve endings
options.B: Document the findings and notify the oncology team promptly to evaluate potential dose modification
options.C: Encourage the patient to soak their hands and feet in very hot water to improve circulation
options.D: Advise the patient to immediately discontinue all prescribed oral analgesics

explanation: Peripheral neuropathy can become irreversible if neurotoxic drugs are continued without dose reduction or cessation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h6)

question: Which laboratory abnormality is a hallmark of tumor lysis syndrome resulting from the rapid breakdown of malignant cells?

options.A: Hypernatremia
options.B: Hypokalemia
options.C: Hyperkalemia
options.D: Hypomagnesemia

explanation: Massive lysis of cancer cells releases large amounts of intracellular potassium into the circulation, causing dangerous hyperkalemia. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h7)

question: A patient with advanced lung cancer presents with facial swelling, distended neck veins, and upper extremity edema. What oncological emergency do these clinical findings suggest?

options.A: Spinal cord compression
options.B: Hypercalcemia of malignancy
options.C: Superior vena cava syndrome
options.D: Febrile neutropenia crisis

explanation: Compression of the superior vena cava impairs venous return from the upper body, producing characteristic facial and upper extremity edema. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of palliative care interventions in advanced cancer management?

options.A: To accelerate the physiological dying process through active medical euthanasia
options.B: To completely eradicate all remaining micrometastatic cancer cells
options.C: To improve the quality of life for patients and their families by managing symptoms
options.D: To reverse bone marrow suppression and stimulate permanent hematopoiesis

explanation: Palliative care prioritizes comfort, symptom relief, and psychosocial support rather than disease eradication. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h8)

question: Which clinical practice is essential when managing chronic cancer pain with opioid analgesics in a palliative care setting?

options.A: Administering opioids around-the-clock to maintain steady therapeutic blood levels
options.B: Switching drug classes daily to prevent rapid development of hepatic tolerance
options.C: Reserving opioid medications exclusively for terminal breakthrough pain episodes
options.D: Withholding pain medication to prevent the inevitable physical addiction of patients

explanation: Scheduled round-the-clock dosing prevents pain from returning, providing more consistent relief than waiting for pain to peak. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h8)

question: What primary practice did Florence Nightingale initiate to improve care for severely wounded soldiers?

options.A: Administering intravenous antibiotics to all trauma admissions
options.B: Isolating infectious patients in separate outdoor tents
options.C: Enforcing mandatory bed rest for seven days post-injury
options.D: Grouping critically injured patients closest to the nursing station

explanation: Placing the most fragile patients nearest to observation points allowed nurses to detect rapid clinical deteriorations immediately. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h1)

question: What is the primary defining characteristic of modern critical care nursing?

options.A: Continuous monitoring and management of life-threatening conditions
options.B: Providing long-term rehabilitation for chronic illnesses
options.C: Delivering palliative care at the end of life
options.D: Focusing exclusively on outpatient surgical recovery

explanation: Critical care units are built around the necessity of uninterrupted physiological observation and rapid intervention for unstable individuals. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which historical event directly drove the creation of specialized respiratory support units in the 1950s?

options.A: Severe cholera epidemics in urban hospitals
options.B: The outbreak of World War II trench warfare
options.C: The global influenza pandemic
options.D: The widespread poliomyelitis outbreaks

explanation: Massive waves of polio paralyzed respiratory muscles, forcing hospitals to centralize patients needing constant breathing assistance. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h2)

question: How did the polio epidemic permanently change hospital organization?

options.A: By eliminating the need for specialized nursing observation
options.B: By proving that mechanical ventilation could be managed safely at home
options.C: By establishing dedicated units for patients requiring intense respiratory support
options.D: By shifting all surgical procedures to outpatient community clinics

explanation: Concentrating patients with identical life-threatening respiratory failure into single wards created the prototype for the modern intensive care unit. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h2)

question: During which decades did multidisciplinary intensive care units become permanent fixtures in hospitals?

options.A: Late 1980s and early 1990s
options.B: Late 1950s and early 1960s
options.C: The turn of the 21st century
options.D: Early 1900s and World War I

explanation: The convergence of surgical advancements, anesthesia development, and respiratory care pushed hospitals to build permanent multidisciplinary ICUs during this era. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h3)

question: A patient is admitted to a newly established multidisciplinary ICU in the 1960s. What major advantage does this unit provide over a general medical ward?

options.A: Guaranteed single-room accommodation for every admitted person
options.B: Completely pain-free recovery without the need for analgesics
options.C: Access to immediate discharge within twenty-four hours
options.D: Concentrated specialized equipment and continuous nursing observation

explanation: Centralizing resources and skilled staff ensures that unstable patients receive immediate, uninterrupted physiological monitoring and intervention. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h3)

question: What was the primary clinical justification for creating specialized Coronary Care Units?

options.A: Surgical repair of blocked coronary arteries required sterile operating suites
options.B: Routine electrocardiograms needed to be performed annually for all adults
options.C: Sudden electrical arrhythmias in heart attack patients could be treated if caught early
options.D: Hypertensive crisis management required specialized isolation rooms

explanation: Continuous heart rhythm monitoring allowed nurses to catch and treat lethal arrhythmias instantly, saving countless lives after myocardial infarctions. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h4)

question: What groundbreaking responsibility did CCU nurses assume with the introduction of cardiac monitors?

options.A: Interpreting cardiac rhythms on monitors and initiating emergency defibrillation
options.B: Performing open-heart bypass surgery independently at the bedside
options.C: Prescribing long-term antiplatelet medications without medical oversight
options.D: Discharging stable cardiac patients within two hours of admission

explanation: Coronary care nursing expanded the traditional scope of practice by empowering nurses to act immediately on life-threatening monitor alarms. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h4)

question: What is a primary purpose of professional critical care nursing organizations?

options.A: Determining national taxation policies for healthcare workers
options.B: Setting educational standards and outlining specific scopes of practice
options.C: Regulating hospital building codes and architectural designs
options.D: Managing pharmaceutical manufacturing and drug pricing

explanation: Specialty organizations protect the public and advance the profession by defining competency requirements and ethical guidelines for practice. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which factor most heavily influenced the transition of critical care from basic nursing to a recognized medical specialty?

options.A: The standardization of patient diets across all hospital departments
options.B: The increasing complexity of unit technology and pharmacological therapies
options.C: The complete elimination of physicians from hospital intensive care units
options.D: The reduction of working hours to four hours per week for all nurses

explanation: Advanced machinery and potent vasoactive drugs required nurses to undergo rigorous specialized training to ensure patient safety. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which of the following is an example of an invasive hemodynamic monitoring tool used in modern intensive care units?

options.A: Pulse oximeter finger probe
options.B: Digital tympanic thermometer
options.C: Arterial catheter
options.D: Standard mercury sphygmomanometer

explanation: Arterial lines provide continuous, beat-to-beat blood pressure measurements directly from inside the vascular system. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why are electronic health records particularly valuable in a modern critical care setting?

options.A: They replace all verbal communication between physicians and nurses
options.B: They track complex physiological trends and highlight subtle signs of clinical decline
options.C: They prevent patients from ever experiencing medication side effects
options.D: They completely remove the need for bedside nursing physical assessments

explanation: Digital systems aggregate vast amounts of continuous data, helping nurses spot deteriorating trends before overt crisis strikes. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is a major focus for the future of critical care nursing in resource-limited environments like Nigeria?

options.A: Relying entirely on imported foreign medical personnel for daily ward operations
options.B: Adapting clinical practices to maintain safety despite equipment shortages
options.C: Eliminating all specialized training programs to reduce administrative costs
options.D: Abandoning mechanical ventilators in favor of manual ventilation exclusively

explanation: Nurses in challenging environments frequently spearhead practical adaptations to deliver safe, effective care with available resources. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h7)

question: A patient is discharged home after surviving a lengthy stay in an intensive care unit. Which modern follow-up initiative specifically addresses their long-term recovery needs?

options.A: Immediate enrollment in professional athletic training
options.B: Post-intensive care syndrome support clinics
options.C: Mandatory cosmetic plastic surgery consultations
options.D: Routine annual dental cleanings and evaluations

explanation: Specialized clinics help manage the physical, cognitive, and psychological impairments survivors often face after critical illness. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary physiological purpose of mechanical ventilation?

options.A: To maintain adequate gas exchange and relieve respiratory muscle work
options.B: To permanently replace damaged lung tissue
options.C: To cure the underlying pulmonary disease
options.D: To directly administer aerosolized systemic antibiotics

explanation: Mechanical ventilation provides supportive care to keep oxygen and carbon dioxide levels stable while the body heals, rather than acting as a curative drug. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h1)

question: Type 2 respiratory failure is primarily characterized by which arterial blood gas abnormality?

options.A: Elevated carbon dioxide tension
options.B: Decreased partial pressure of oxygen
options.C: Decreased arterial pH with high oxygen levels
options.D: Significantly elevated oxygen saturation

explanation: Type 2 failure is ventilatory failure, meaning the lungs fail to eliminate carbon dioxide effectively, leading to hypercapnia. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h1)

question: What does PEEP stand for in mechanical ventilation settings?

options.A: Peak external expiratory phase
options.B: Positive end-expiratory pressure
options.C: Pulmonary elastic equalization pressure
options.D: Primary endotracheal exchange pathway

explanation: PEEP maintains a baseline of pressure above atmospheric pressure at the end of exhalation to prevent alveolar collapse and improve oxygenation. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h2)

question: Why is tidal volume calculation typically based on a patient's ideal body weight rather than their actual measured weight?

options.A: To simplify nursing charting calculations during emergency admissions
options.B: To prevent barotrauma and volutrauma caused by overdistending normal lung tissue in obese individuals
options.C: To account for fluid retention and edema in the extremities
options.D: To ensure the ventilator consumes less electrical power during long shifts

explanation: Lung size correlates with height rather than total body mass, so using actual weight in obese patients can deliver dangerously large air volumes and damage lung tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of immediate epigastric and chest auscultation after endotracheal intubation?

options.A: To measure the exact tidal volume delivered by the machine
options.B: To verify that the tube has not inadvertently entered the esophagus
options.C: To clear thick secretions from the mainstem bronchi
options.D: To calculate the patient's baseline respiratory compliance

explanation: Listening over the epigastrium and lungs immediately checks that air enters the lungs rather than the stomach, preventing fatal hypoxia. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h3)

question: A newly intubated patient is placed on a ventilator, and the low-pressure alarm begins sounding continuously while abdominal distention is noted. What immediate action should the nurse take?

options.A: Instill sterile water down the endotracheal tube to clear a mucus plug
options.B: Prepare for immediate re-intubation because esophageal placement is likely
options.C: Increase the ventilator respiratory rate to compensate for missing breaths
options.D: Silence the alarm permanently and document the machine settings

explanation: Abdominal distention combined with low pressure alarms strongly indicates that air is going into the stomach through an esophageal tube rather than the lungs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h3)

question: How does positive pressure mechanical ventilation directly impact a patient's cardiovascular status?

options.A: It prevents fluid overload by squeezing blood out of the peripheral vasculature
options.B: It has no measurable effect on blood pressure or heart rate
options.C: It increases intrathoracic pressure, which can reduce venous return and lower blood pressure
options.D: It directly stimulates myocardial contraction to increase cardiac output

explanation: High pressure inside the chest cavity compresses the vena cava, decreasing blood flow back to the heart and potentially causing hypotension. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the clinical purpose of utilizing sedation scoring tools like the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale for ventilated patients?

options.A: To determine the precise time frame for surgical tracheostomy placement
options.B: To maintain optimal comfort, prevent accidental extubation, and avoid over-sedation
options.C: To calculate the exact caloric requirements for enteral feeding pumps
options.D: To measure the mechanical resistance of the lung parenchyma

explanation: Sedation scales guide clinicians to provide just enough medication to keep the patient safe and comfortable without delaying weaning. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the maximum recommended duration for a single pass of endotracheal suctioning?

options.A: Two to three minutes
options.B: One full minute
options.C: 30 to 45 seconds
options.D: 10 to 15 seconds

explanation: Limiting suction duration prevents prolonged oxygen deprivation and subsequent cardiac arrhythmias during the procedure. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why is routine instillation of normal saline directly into the endotracheal tube before suctioning generally discouraged?

options.A: It permanently ruins the electronic sensors inside the ventilator tubing
options.B: It causes immediate collapse of the mainstem bronchi
options.C: It neutralizes the action of prescribed pulmonary medications
options.D: It can cause oxygen desaturation and drive bacteria deeper into the lower respiratory tract

explanation: Evidence shows routine saline instillation does not thin secretions effectively, but it does increase infection risks and drops oxygen levels. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h5)

question: What is the recommended angle for elevating the head of the bed to help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?

options.A: 60 to 90 degrees sitting upright
options.B: 0 degrees strictly flat
options.C: 30 to 45 degrees
options.D: 10 to 15 degrees slight tilt

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed uses gravity to reduce the risk of gastric contents and oral secretions pooling above the cuff and micro-aspirating into the lungs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h6)

question: Which complication is most directly associated with high inspiratory pressures overdistending the alveoli in mechanically ventilated patients?

options.A: Peripheral neuropathy of the lower limbs
options.B: Barotrauma resulting in pneumothorax
options.C: Renal tubular necrosis and oliguria
options.D: Severe metabolic alkalosis

explanation: Excessive pressure pops fragile alveolar walls, allowing air to leak into the pleural space and collapse the lung. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h6)

question: What assessment finding is considered a sign of failure during a spontaneous breathing trial?

options.A: A calm, cooperative demeanor with stable vital signs
options.B: Heart rate and respiratory rate increasing significantly beyond baseline limits
options.C: Normal blood pressure and warm, dry skin
options.D: Adequate urine output of over 30 milliliters per hour

explanation: Tachycardia, tachypnea, and distress indicate the patient's respiratory muscles are fatiguing and they are not yet ready to breathe independently. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h7)

question: At what specific respiratory cycle point should an endotracheal tube be pulled out during an extubation procedure?

options.A: At peak inspiration
options.B: During a prolonged breath hold
options.C: Midway through a passive sigh breath
options.D: At the end of expiration

explanation: Removing the tube at peak inspiration ensures air flows outward through the vocal cords, sweeping loose secretions away from the lower airway as the tube comes out. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h7)

question: Which strategy is most effective for helping a conscious, intubated patient communicate their needs at the bedside?

options.A: Restraining the patient's hands to prevent frantic gestures
options.B: Insisting that the patient whisper words loudly through the tube cuff
options.C: Providing a magic slate, picture board, or alphabet communication chart
options.D: Temporarily deflating the endotracheal tube cuff whenever they look frustrated

explanation: Alternative visual and tactile communication tools bypass the blocked vocal cords, reducing the severe psychological distress of voicelessness. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h8)

question: Why is psychological support for both the patient and their family an essential component of mechanical ventilation management?

options.A: Psychological support replaces the need for pharmacological sedation entirely
options.B: Intubation and critical care environments frequently trigger severe anxiety, delirium, and trauma
options.C: Anxiety directly increases the mechanical compliance of lung tissue
options.D: Family members are legally required to operate ventilator alarm systems

explanation: The ICU experience leaves lasting emotional scars, and active support mitigates delirium, panic, and post-intensive care syndrome. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of an emergency crash cart in a clinical setting?

options.A: To store routine daily medications for stable ward patients
options.B: To provide immediate access to life-saving tools during acute collapse
options.C: To transport laboratory specimens safely to the hospital laboratory
options.D: To house administrative documents and patient charts securely

explanation: Crash carts contain pre-checked resuscitative devices and emergency medications designed for rapid deployment during acute crises like cardiac arrest. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why is immediate access to functioning resuscitative equipment critical during an emergency?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any documentation during the shift
options.B: It prevents prolonged tissue hypoxia and irreversible organ damage
options.C: It allows junior staff to practice procedural skills unsupervised
options.D: It reduces the financial burden of extended hospital stays

explanation: Rapid intervention restores perfusion and oxygenation quickly, halting cellular death in vital organs like the brain and heart. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which airway device is generally contraindicated in a patient with severe facial trauma or suspected basilar skull fracture?

options.A: Bag-valve-mask device
options.B: Nasopharyngeal airway
options.C: Endotracheal tube
options.D: Oropharyngeal airway

explanation: Passing a tube through the nose when a skull fracture is present risks intracranial placement of the device. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary function of an oropharyngeal airway during basic life support?

options.A: To suction thick pulmonary secretions from the main bronchi
options.B: To displace the tongue away from the posterior pharyngeal wall
options.C: To measure continuous end-tidal carbon dioxide levels accurately
options.D: To deliver high-flow humidified oxygen directly to the lungs

explanation: Unconscious patients lose muscle tone, causing the tongue to fall backward and block the airway; an OPA physically lifts it out of the way. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary difference between an automated external defibrillator and a manual defibrillator?

options.A: Manual defibrillators require the operator to interpret the heart rhythm and select the energy dose
options.B: Automated external defibrillators require complex surgical insertion of internal chest leads
options.C: Automated external defibrillators can only be used by certified physician specialists
options.D: Manual defibrillators do not deliver electrical shocks to the myocardium

explanation: Clinicians operating manual units must analyze the ECG tracing and manually dial in the appropriate joules, unlike AEDs which automate these steps. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h3)

question: When is an intraosseous access needle typically chosen over a peripheral intravenous line during a critical resuscitation?

options.A: When the nurse prefers a painless route for routine antibiotic administration
options.B: When the patient has stable blood pressure and easily visible peripheral veins
options.C: When the physician wants to avoid monitoring the patient's central venous pressure
options.D: When peripheral venous access is impossible due to severe circulatory collapse

explanation: Bone marrow vascular spaces do not collapse during shock, providing a reliable alternative route when peripheral veins cannot be cannulated. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h3)

question: How often should a comprehensive check of the emergency crash cart typically be performed in an inpatient ward?

options.A: At every nursing shift change
options.B: Only after a patient experiences cardiac arrest
options.C: Whenever new staff members are hired
options.D: Once every calendar month

explanation: Routine checks during shift handovers guarantee that missing items, dead batteries, or expired drugs are identified and replaced immediately. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard component of routine crash cart maintenance?

options.A: Checking expiration dates on emergency drugs and sterile supplies
options.B: Testing the defibrillator battery functionality and screen display
options.C: Calibrating the internal mechanical components of the infusion pumps
options.D: Verifying the suction machine produces adequate negative pressure

explanation: Biomedical engineering departments handle complex calibration of infusion pumps on a scheduled preventative maintenance cycle, not during routine daily nursing crash cart checks. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h4)

question: What is a primary sign that a suction machine is failing to generate adequate negative pressure during airway clearance?

options.A: The collection canister fills rapidly with sterile water
options.B: The pressure gauge needle points toward the highest red warning zone
options.C: The machine motor emits a loud, high-pitched mechanical whirring sound
options.D: Secretions are not effectively cleared from the patient's pharynx

explanation: Inadequate suction pressure directly impairs the device's ability to pull fluids and mucus through the tubing. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h5)

question: A nurse is ventilating an adult patient with a bag-valve-mask device and notices the bag is extremely hard to compress. What should be checked first?

options.A: The expiration date printed on the exterior cardboard box
options.B: Whether the oxygen cylinder pressure gauge reads empty
options.C: If the patient's airway is obstructed or the valve is stuck
options.D: The battery level indicator on the nearby cardiac monitor

explanation: Stiff resistance during BVM squeezing typically points to an airway obstruction, incorrect head position, or a malfunctioning one-way valve. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h5)

question: What is the primary statutory body responsible for regulating nursing education and practice in Nigeria?

options.A: Federal Ministry of Health
options.B: National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives
options.C: Nigerian Medical and Dental Council
options.D: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: The NMCN is the statutory body established by law to regulate nursing and midwifery education, registration, and professional practice across the country. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why is a thorough understanding of legal frameworks particularly critical for nurses working in an Intensive Care Unit?

options.A: Hospital management policies always supersede national nursing legislation in emergency wards
options.B: ICU interventions frequently involve complex life-sustaining measures that border on bodily intrusion
options.C: Criminal liability does not apply to healthcare workers in specialized units
options.D: Critical care nurses operate completely independently without physician oversight

explanation: Because critical care involves invasive procedures and high-stakes life support, practitioners face unique legal scrutiny regarding consent and boundary violations. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h1)

question: What term describes the legal obligation of a nurse to answer for their professional actions and clinical decisions?

options.A: Exemptive autonomy
options.B: Strict liability
options.C: Professional accountability
options.D: Vicarious immunity

explanation: Accountability requires clinicians to take responsibility for the direct consequences of their clinical decisions and nursing care delivery. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h2)

question: A critical care nurse independently administers an unprescribed restricted vasopressor to stabilize a crashing patient. What legal issue does this action primarily raise?

options.A: Violating institutional documentation guidelines
options.B: Failing to activate the emergency response team
options.C: Breaching patient confidentiality regulations
options.D: Exceeding the legal scope of nursing practice

explanation: Administering restricted medications without a formal medical order or approved protocol breaches the legal boundaries defining professional nursing practice in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which legal principle allows clinicians to provide emergency life-saving treatment to an unconscious patient without explicit consent?

options.A: The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur
options.B: The emergency doctrine
options.C: The principle of beneficence
options.D: Vicarious liability

explanation: The emergency doctrine legally shields providers when urgent intervention is necessary to prevent death or permanent injury and obtaining consent is impossible. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h3)

question: A fully conscious and oriented patient admitted to the ICU explicitly refuses mechanical ventilation after being informed of the risks. What is the most appropriate initial nursing response?

options.A: Respect the refusal, document the conversation, and notify the attending physician immediately
options.B: Ask family members to override the patient's decision so treatment can begin
options.C: Proceed with intubation anyway because the ICU environment dictates life preservation
options.D: Administer a mild sedative to calm the patient and insert the breathing tube

explanation: Competent adults retain the legal right to autonomous bodily integrity and can refuse any medical treatment, including life-saving interventions. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h3)

question: What legal document allows competent individuals to state their preferences for medical care before losing decision-making capacity?

options.A: Advanced directive
options.B: Scope of practice charter
options.C: Incident report
options.D: Malpractice waiver

explanation: Advanced directives guide future healthcare decisions when a patient becomes incapacitated through illness or injury. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h4)

question: Which statement best distinguishes the withdrawal of futile life support from active euthanasia?

options.A: Withdrawing futile care allows the underlying disease process to take its natural course, whereas euthanasia involves an intentional act to end life.
options.B: There is no legal or clinical distinction between withholding life support and administering a lethal dose of medication.
options.C: Active euthanasia is legally sanctioned in all Nigerian critical care units, whereas withdrawing treatment is strictly prohibited.
options.D: Withdrawing care requires court authorization in every single instance, unlike voluntary euthanasia.

explanation: Withdrawing burdensome, non-beneficial interventions permits natural death, whereas euthanasia requires a direct, active lethal intervention. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the accepted method for correcting a written charting error in a paper nursing record?

options.A: Scratch out the incorrect text heavily until it is completely unreadable
options.B: Draw a single line through the error, write 'error' alongside it, sign and date
options.C: Apply correction fluid generously over the mistake and write the correct text on top
options.D: Tear out the entire page and rewrite the nursing notes cleanly

explanation: Maintaining transparency requires that the original entry remains legible underneath a single strike-through, accompanied by an explanatory note and signature. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h5)

question: Why is contemporaneous documentation considered crucial for legal protection in critical care nursing?

options.A: Hospital management uses the charts exclusively to calculate monthly staff salaries
options.B: Patients have a legal right to burn their nursing records upon discharge
options.C: Late entries completely eliminate the possibility of a malpractice lawsuit
options.D: Written records serve as objective, legal evidence of the timing and quality of care delivered

explanation: Contemporaneous charts provide an immutable timeline of clinical events, protecting both patient and nurse by verifying that timely interventions occurred. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h5)

question: What is the first essential legal element that must be established to prove nursing negligence?

options.A: Failure to document in the chart
options.B: Absence of a physician supervisor
options.C: Intentional desire to cause harm
options.D: Existence of a duty of care

explanation: A malpractice claim cannot proceed unless the plaintiff first establishes that an established professional relationship created a legal duty of care. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h6)

question: Which of the following scenarios describes a classic case of nursing malpractice in a critical care setting?

options.A: Refusing to accept a verbal order from a doctor because the medication dose is missing
options.B: Failing to monitor an infusing inotropic medication, leading to extravasation and severe tissue necrosis
options.C: Reporting a failing equipment monitor to the biomedical engineering department
options.D: Consulting the hospital ethics committee regarding a disputed family surrogate decision

explanation: This scenario demonstrates a clear breach of standard monitoring protocols that directly results in physical injury to the patient. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h6)

question: What is a primary responsibility of a nurse acting as a patient advocate in the intensive care unit?

options.A: Safeguarding the rights, safety, and welfare of the vulnerable patient
options.B: Ensuring hospital financial profitability during resource allocation
options.C: Following all medical orders blindly without questioning potential risks
options.D: Acting as the primary legal counsel for the patient's family

explanation: Advocacy centers on protecting the patient's best interests, rights, and safety, especially when they cannot speak for themselves. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h7)

question: What should a critical care nurse do when faced with a clinical directive that clearly compromises patient safety?

options.A: Chain of command escalation to address the unsafe order
options.B: Discuss the doctor's mistake openly on social media platforms
options.C: Ignore the situation entirely and leave the shift early
options.D: Execute the order immediately to avoid conflict with senior physicians

explanation: Patient safety and professional accountability require the nurse to challenge unsafe directives through appropriate institutional channels. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary focus of critical care delivered within community and primary health settings?

options.A: Providing specialized intensive care unit technology at home
options.B: Conducting major surgical operations in rural clinics
options.C: Long-term rehabilitation of chronic terminal illnesses
options.D: Early recognition of instability and prompt stabilization

explanation: Community critical care prioritizes identifying deteriorating patients early and stabilizing them before transport since advanced ICU tech is absent. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why does community critical care rely more heavily on clinical intuition and structured assessments than hospital care?

options.A: Patients in the community present with milder symptoms
options.B: Community nurses work completely independently of protocols
options.C: Advanced diagnostic laboratories are always available on site
options.D: Rural clinics typically lack complex monitoring technology

explanation: The absence of advanced hospital monitors forces community nurses to depend on systematic physical assessments and clinical judgment. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h1)

question: What are the primary drivers of critical illness presentations in Nigerian community healthcare settings?

options.A: Occupational hazards specific to office workers
options.B: Infectious diseases, trauma, and acute complications
options.C: Chronic autoimmune conditions requiring chemotherapy
options.D: Congenital disorders and rare metabolic syndromes

explanation: Conditions like severe malaria, injuries from road accidents, and acute dehydration dominate the emergency case load in Nigerian primary centers. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h2)

question: How do financial constraints and distance from tertiary facilities impact patients experiencing critical emergencies in rural Nigeria?

options.A: Individuals frequently present in late-stage shock or organ failure
options.B: Community clinics automatically cover all emergency treatment costs
options.C: Patients arrive earlier because they can afford private transport
options.D: Families bypass traditional healers to seek immediate hospital care

explanation: Delays caused by out-of-pocket costs and geographical barriers mean patients often reach care only when their condition has deteriorated drastically. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of utilizing a structured triage system in a primary health clinic?

options.A: To diagnose the specific underlying disease process immediately
options.B: To calculate the exact financial cost of required emergency drugs
options.C: To ensure that patients are served strictly on a first-come basis
options.D: To categorize patients based on clinical urgency and acuity

explanation: Triage ensures that individuals with life-threatening instability receive immediate attention regardless of when they arrived at the facility. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h3)

question: A patient arrives at a rural clinic gasping for air, using accessory neck muscles, and with a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per minute. According to primary assessment principles, which parameter is immediately compromised?

options.A: Exposure
options.B: Breathing
options.C: Disability
options.D: Circulation

explanation: An elevated respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, and respiratory distress directly indicate an acute compromise of the breathing component. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h3)

question: What is the absolute first priority during the emergency stabilization of a critically ill patient?

options.A: Establishing intravenous access
options.B: Obtaining a detailed family history
options.C: Administering broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.D: Securing a patent airway

explanation: The ABCDE protocol dictates that airway management always comes first because a blocked airway leads to rapid death within minutes. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h4)

question: What alternative vascular access technique should a nurse consider when peripheral veins are completely collapsed in a severely shocked patient?

options.A: Intraosseous cannulation
options.B: Continuous oral rehydration therapy
options.C: Subcutaneous fluid infusion
options.D: Intramuscular injection of saline

explanation: When peripheral veins are inaccessible due to profound vasoconstriction, intraosseous access provides a rapid and reliable route for fluids and medications. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h4)

question: Which medication class is administered immediately to halt prolonged seizure activity during an episode of status epilepticus?

options.A: Antihistamines
options.B: Opioid analgesics
options.C: Beta-blockers
options.D: Benzodiazepines

explanation: Fast-acting benzodiazepines like diazepam or lorazepam are the first-line pharmacological agents used to stop continuous seizure activity safely. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h5)

question: A patient presents to a primary health post with severe respiratory distress, wheezing, and an inability to complete sentences due to breathlessness. What is the most appropriate immediate community intervention?

options.A: Administering a short-acting beta-agonist bronchodilator
options.B: Placing the patient in a flat supine position to rest
options.C: Instructing the patient to perform deep breathing exercises
options.D: Setting up a continuous intravenous antibiotic infusion

explanation: Acute bronchospasm in asthma requires immediate bronchodilator therapy to open the airways and relieve severe respiratory distress. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h5)

question: How can a nurse ensure safe fluid administration when an electronic infusion pump is unavailable in a rural clinic?

options.A: Allowing intravenous fluids to flow freely without any flow regulation
options.B: Switching entirely to intramuscular injections for all fluid needs
options.C: Squeezing the plastic IV bag manually to speed up medication delivery
options.D: Using a microdrip chamber set combined with careful hourly monitoring
